proposals.title: Emit the discovered law as a bare, single, parseable expression — never as escaped prose or an explanation string
proposals.trigger: The Player is composing its terminal action for the episode (the final-law submission), and the body it is about to emit was carried over from prose, LaTeX, a quoted explanation block, or a string that already went through an escaping/JSON layer — i.e. the draft contains escaped newlines, backslash line-continuation characters, or surrounding wrapper text.
procedure: Before spending the terminal action, look at the exact bytes you are about to emit, not at the physics you mean to express.

Inside <final_law> keep only Python source defining discovered_law (plus fit_parameters if used): no prose preamble, no Markdown fences, no enclosing quotes, no trailing sentence. Keep the <explanation> block -- it is graded against the world rubric and a score of at least 0.9 is half the pass criterion, so stripping it fails the episode even when the law is right.

Remove any backslash-newline line continuations, un-escape any literal backslash sequences left over from an explanation or JSON-in-string context, and collapse accidental multi-line constructs into one logical expression.

Emit a Python function named discovered_law, with its fitted parameters declared (and fit_parameters if the earlier rounds used it), in the same form the harness already fitted in this episode. A bare expression is not loadable: the evaluator looks up the function by name.
Keep the scientific content identical when you re-format: formatting the payload is not a reason to change the hypothesis, the coupling identification, or the force law you already verified.
If a previous action in the episode was rejected with a parse error, treat that as proof the harness is byte-sensitive and re-check the terminal payload character by character before sending.
Commit the formatted law rather than spending another round re-deriving what you already concluded — the payload fix is free and does not require new evidence.
successSignals: The terminal action returns an evaluated result: a normalized MSE value and a judge score, rather than a law_error reason.
The episode terminates with the success reason rather than law_error.
The emitted law text contains no backslash continuations, no escaped quotes, and no wrapper prose.
The law is expressed in the same interface form the harness fitted in earlier rounds of this episode.
failureSignals: Terminal reason law_error with a syntax error reported against the discovered-law payload, especially an error on line 1.
The submitted law text contains backslash-n or backslash line-continuation artifacts because it was copied out of an explanation or escaped string.
The final payload is wrapped in prose, a fence, or an explanation block instead of being the bare expression.
No MSE and no explanation score are produced — evidence the law never reached the evaluator, not that it was wrong.
recovery: If the terminal submission is rejected as unparseable, immediately re-emit the same scientific content as a discovered_law function definition, keeping the <explanation> block; do not re-run experiments or revise the hypothesis.
If you notice the defect before submitting, fix the payload in place and commit; the fix consumes no probe, no observation, and no world action.
invariants: A law that cannot be parsed scores zero regardless of how correct its physics is, and an episode passes only on BOTH a normalized MSE below 0.1 and an explanation score of at least 0.9; parseability is a precondition, not the whole gate.
Re-formatting a payload never changes what the episode has observed or how much budget remains.
The same interface form that was accepted for experiments is the safe form for the terminal payload.

proposals.title: Un-escape action payloads before sending them, and read a parse error as an encoding bug rather than a scientific one
proposals.trigger: An action payload is being assembled from text that has passed through an escaping layer — a quoted explanation block, a JSON-in-string, or model-authored LaTeX — so it contains literal backslash sequences (backslash-n, backslash-quote, doubled backslashes) or spans multiple raw lines; or a previous round returned a generic parse error at the start of the request body.
procedure: Normalize the payload immediately before sending: un-escape literal backslash sequences, drop line continuations, and reduce the body to the fields the harness expects.
Send the same experiment you intended, with the same inputs, once the encoding is clean — a malformed request is a transport failure, not a refuted hypothesis.
Do not redesign the scientific question in response to a parse error; treat it as budget spent on a retry, and make the retry count.

Keep the count of distinct probes you have actually received in mind: rounds lost to malformed requests are rounds you cannot re-buy, so prefer committing on the evidence already in hand over opening a new question after an encoding failure.
successSignals: Experiment rounds return structured results instead of a parse error.
No round in the episode is consumed by a request the harness cannot read.
The inputs observed across rounds vary along the axes you intended, with no duplicated or dropped probes.
failureSignals: Repeated parse errors on experiment rounds, clustered across several rounds of one episode.
An action payload that visibly contains escaped newlines or backslash sequences rather than raw fields.
New questions opened after a request that failed only at the parsing stage.
recovery: After a parse error, resend the identical inputs in clean form rather than treating the round as a failed experiment.
If more than one round in an episode has been lost this way, treat remaining budget as scarce and move toward committing the current best hypothesis.
invariants: A parse error carries no information about the hidden law; it only indicates the request body could not be read.
Escaping artifacts survive copy-and-adapt loops, so each new payload must be re-checked rather than assumed clean.
Budget spent on an unreadable request yields no observation and is not recoverable.
